entries.title: Unmatched royalties
entries.take: Money a collector has received for a use of music but cannot yet tie to a specific song or owner. The MLC counts it inside unclaimed accrued royalties once the holding period ends.

entries.title: Unclaimed royalties
entries.take: Everyday word for money no owner has collected. Collectives use it loosely, so check whether a page means unmatched money, or money for an owner who has been identified but not found.

entries.title: Black box
entries.take: Informal industry name for a pool of collected royalties that nobody has been able to allocate. It is a nickname, not a legal or official term; collectives use names such as suspense account.

entries.title: Suspense account
entries.take: The ledger a collective uses to park royalties when the works in a usage report have not been identified. Societies review it for reasonableness before each distribution.

entries.title: Most unmatched money starts with thin usage reports
entries.take: The commonest cause the surveyed societies gave: a service reports the recording but nothing about the song, its writers or its publishers.
entries.body: A 2020 survey for the Copyright Office, based on anonymous replies from collectives worldwide, ranks the reasons money cannot be matched. Top of the list are reports that name only the recording, data that cannot be matched by machine and still needs manual research, and works the owner never registered. Better registered data on your side shrinks the gap.
do: Register each song and recording wherever it earns, with writers, shares and identifiers.
Check that recording codes and song codes agree across your distributor and your registrations.

entries.title: Conflicting registrations and unknown shares hold money back
entries.take: Money can sit unpaid when two registrations disagree, when shares are unknown or total over 100 percent, or when an ownership dispute is open.
entries.body: The surveyed societies also named multiple registrations with conflicting data, missing proof of who controls a work, unverified registrations and unresolved disputes. The MLC's Overclaims Tool exists for the case where claimed shares add to more than the whole. A dispute over who owns a song is a matter for a music lawyer, not a registration form.
do: Agree splits in writing with co-writers before anyone registers.
Compare what each publisher and society holds for the same song.

entries.title: A song can be known at home and missing abroad
entries.take: Societies often lack a foreign owner's details, or hold data from another society that is incomplete, so foreign income can stall.
entries.body: Societies learn about works from their own members, from sister societies under reciprocal agreements and from shared databases. The survey lists missing foreign interested-party information and incomplete data from other societies among the causes. If your sub-publisher or society abroad lacks your song, income there may sit unallocated.
do: Ask your society which sister societies hold your works.
Ask your sub-publisher which territories have your registrations.

entries.title: No account with the collector, no payment
entries.take: SoundExchange pays only registered owners and artists, and the MLC keeps a list of owners who have not joined. Societies generally pay members or affiliates.
entries.body: SoundExchange says artists and sound recording owners must register to receive digital performance royalties. The MLC publishes a lookup of rightsholders who may be owed money and have not joined. The CMO survey adds that societies typically pay their own members and affiliates. Not being known to the collector is the simplest reason money goes unclaimed.
do: Register with each collector that pays your kind of income.
Search each collector's list for your name.

entries.title: Letting contact and bank details go stale
entries.take: Societies list missing current addresses and bank details among the reasons identified owners still go unpaid.
entries.body: A work can be matched to a known owner and still be unpaid because the collector cannot reach that owner or has no valid payment details. The survey also notes rights withdrawn from a society while the database was never updated. After a move, a name change or a change of publisher, update every account.
do: Update address, bank and tax details after any change.
Tell each society in writing when rights move.

entries.title: No collective matches everything
entries.take: The survey author says a claim of a perfect match rate deserves doubt, and that high 80s percent on current service data is generally seen as very good.
entries.body: This is the report author's account of conversations with executives, not a measured benchmark. Her point is that a share of reported usage will always stay unmatched, so owners should not assume that a missing line on a statement is a mistake by them. Check, then claim.
do: Treat unmatched usage as normal and check for it on a schedule.

entries.title: Search the MLC's list of owners who have not joined
entries.take: Search your name, or the name you collect royalties under, in the Missing Member Lookup. If you appear, join the MLC. The page says connecting is free.
entries.body: The lookup covers US digital audio mechanical royalties for rightsholders who are not yet members. It leaves out historical unmatched royalties, which the MLC treats separately. Try each name variant you have used, including the name on your song registrations.
do: Search every name and alias you have used.
Join the MLC if your name appears.

entries.title: US law makes the MLC list unmatched works and give notice
entries.take: The statute requires a public place to see unmatched works and claim them, and industry notice of a payout at least 90 days ahead.
entries.body: Section 115 requires the MLC to keep an online facility with its contact details showing works, or shares of works, it could not match, where an owner can assert a claim. It must also make good-faith efforts to announce to the industry a coming payout of unclaimed money, with interest, at least 90 days ahead. Watch for those notices.
do: Check the MLC's unmatched list and distribution notices as they appear.

entries.title: Check SoundExchange's lists, register, then claim recordings
entries.take: If you have not registered, use SoundExchange's search tool to see whether you are owed. Registration is free, and SX Direct is used to search and claim recordings.
entries.body: SoundExchange collects US digital performance royalties for sound recordings on non-interactive services. Its page keeps four lists of unregistered or partly registered creators. The page does not set out a claim deadline or what becomes of money nobody claims, so ask SoundExchange directly about older plays.
do: Search the unregistered lists for your name and recordings.
Register, then use SX Direct to claim recordings.

entries.title: SoundExchange's four status lists for unclaimed royalties
entries.take: SoundExchange sorts creators with royalties waiting into four lists. Knowing which one fits you shows what is missing.
rows: Unregistered Artists
No registration, or the registered parties have not made a complete claim
Partially Unregistered Artists
Only some performers of a group are registered; others are still missing
Unregistered Performers
No current registration for these individuals
Unregistered Sound Recording Owners
No registration, or the registered party has not made a full claim

entries.title: In Canada, match recordings in CMRRA's unclaimed works portal
entries.take: Get a CMRRA Direct account, then use the Unclaimed Works menu to match recordings or add missing ownership shares for online service uses in Canada.
entries.body: CMRRA says approval of a new account can take up to 3 business days. After it verifies a submission, its usual quarterly invoicing covers current and past use of the recording. The page names no fee or deadline. Details such as the footnote on the menu item were not on the page, so confirm them with CMRRA.
do: Apply for CMRRA Direct before you need to claim.
Keep the share evidence ready for each claim.

entries.title: In the UK, add yourself to a recording's line-up through myPPL
entries.take: If you played on a recording but are not on its line-up, submit a performer claim in myPPL and choose your role. PPL may ask for evidence.
entries.body: PPL says an audible contribution generally counts, and some roles do not pay. Studio producers use a separate form that the featured performers must also complete. If the track is not on PPL's database, ask the rightsholder to add it. Qualification depends on where the performance happened or where the performer lived or held citizenship.
do: List your role, dates and the recording details before you submit.
Ask the label to add a missing track.

entries.title: Societies post lists of unidentified works, but not always openly
entries.take: Many societies publish unidentified works on their sites, some only above a money threshold, and some only to members or affiliates.
entries.body: The survey found posting lists of unidentified works to be the commonest outreach method. One example threshold was works earning $100 or more. Since societies usually pay members and affiliates, such lists may be open to them alone. Publishers often get bulk access that songwriters lack. Ask your own society where its list is.
do: Ask each society if it posts a list and who may see it.

entries.title: Where to check for unclaimed money, by country and type of income
entries.take: Four places that publish a way to check or claim: the MLC, SoundExchange, CMRRA and PPL. Each covers a different kind of income.
rows: The MLC (US)
Digital mechanicals for owners not yet joined
Search the Missing Member Lookup, then join
SoundExchange (US)
Digital performance royalties for recordings
Search its lists, register, claim in SX Direct
CMRRA (Canada)
Online service uses of unmatched recordings and shares
Open a CMRRA Direct account, use Unclaimed Works
PPL (UK)
Performer income for recordings
Claim a line-up place in myPPL

entries.title: Collectives match in layers, and spend manual effort where money is
entries.take: Societies run automated matching, then manual research, and often reserve the manual step for works above a value or usage level, such as $10.
entries.body: The survey describes matching against work and recording codes plus titles and names, with manual research afterwards and quality checks. Some societies match recordings to works before service reports arrive. Audio fingerprinting is used less often. For small amounts, the cost of research can exceed what it recovers, so low earners may wait longest.

entries.title: Identifiers let a collective link your song to you
entries.take: Societies lean on the ISWC for the song, the IPI number for the person and the ISRC for the recording to link a report to a payee.
entries.body: WIPO's music module describes the ISWC as the reference number for a work, tied to rights holders in the IPI system. The survey says societies use ISRC, ISWC and IPI alongside titles and names. Registrations that carry these codes give a collector more to match on.
do: Add your IPI number and song codes to registrations where the form asks.

entries.title: What collectives do with royalties they cannot allocate
entries.take: The survey lists several methods that societies use or have used. Practice varies by society and by type of income, so ask your own.
rows: Share to the same pool
Held over and shared among current earners of the next distribution
Pro rata to paid owners
Split among those paid from the same source in the same period
Allocate by work
Sorted by work first, then by each owner's share
Send to a foreign society
A work known to be foreign goes to the society in that country
Pay the current owner
If the owner at the time is unknown, the present owner is paid
Cover costs or fund causes
Used for operating costs or for shared member benefits

entries.title: Most surveyed societies do not use US-style market share
entries.take: The MLC's statutory market-share method is not the usual approach abroad: the surveyed societies most often use other ways to share out money.
entries.body: US law tells the MLC to share unclaimed accrued royalties by relative market share. The survey says participating societies most often do not use owner market share, and one method it lists works by catalogue. Do not assume a society abroad pays out unclaimed money to larger owners.
do: Ask each foreign society how it distributes undistributed income.

entries.title: Some societies deduct for cultural and social funds
entries.take: Many continental European and Latin American societies divert part of collections to social, cultural or educational purposes. WIPO says they need prior agreement.
entries.body: The survey calls the practice controversial when sums are large, unclear or taken from foreign rights holders. WIPO's module states that these deductions are not cost recovery, so rights holders and other societies have to agree to them beforehand. CISAC's collection figures are reported before such deductions.
do: Check a society's deduction rules before choosing where to register.

entries.title: US study: known owners who cannot be found should be held for
entries.take: The Copyright Office recommended that money for an owner who is identified but not located be held until that owner is found, and that market shares be independently verified.
entries.body: This adds to the five-year holding advice covered elsewhere in this guide. These are recommendations the MLC must weigh substantially, not rules. Check the MLC's own current policy before relying on them.
do: Compare the MLC's current policy with the recommendations.

entries.title: Gather identity and ownership papers before you claim
entries.take: Societies commonly ask for legal name and aliases, contact and tax details, identity documents and proof of ownership or splits for each work.
entries.body: The survey lists what collectives may require: full names and pseudonyms, ID codes, role and share, contact details, proof of identity, tax numbers and documents proving rights by territory. Having them in one folder speeds every claim.
do: Collect agreements, split sheets and ID in one folder.
Note every alias used on past releases.

entries.title: Claim in a fixed order: find, register, claim, then follow up
entries.take: Each body works the same way: search its list, register or join, claim the song or recording, then watch for the payment and ask when none comes.
entries.body: The MLC separates a Claiming Tool for partly claimed songs, a Matching Tool for unmatched recordings and registration tools for missing songs. SoundExchange, CMRRA and PPL each ask for registration before a claim. Wait times are not promised on these pages.
do: Do the same four steps for each collector.
Diary a check on each claim.

entries.title: Assuming one registration covers every collector
entries.take: A PRO account, an MLC account and a SoundExchange account are separate. Each pays only what it collects, so a missing registration leaves money unclaimed.
entries.body: SoundExchange requires its own registration for digital performance royalties. The MLC's lookup lists owners not yet in the MLC. Societies abroad typically pay their own members and affiliates. Check each income type separately.
do: List every collector for each kind of income you earn.

entries.title: Claiming the whole song when you share it
entries.take: Claim only your own share. Shares that total more than the whole create an overclaim, which freezes payment while the owners sort it out.
entries.body: The MLC's Overclaims Tool lets owners change or give up shares, contact each other and upload documents. Societies abroad also list conflicting claims as a cause of unpaid money. Disputed ownership is a matter for a music lawyer.
do: Confirm splits with co-writers before claiming.
See a music lawyer if ownership is disputed.

entries.title: Do not assume a deadline, and do not assume time is unlimited
entries.take: The CMRRA, PPL and SoundExchange pages read here name no claim deadline. The MLC's April 2027 date starts distributions and is not a cut-off.
entries.body: Silence on a page is not a promise. PPL notes the 70-year term of the performer right, and the MLC will share remaining money by market share from April 2027, so claiming early protects you. Ask each collector in writing how long it holds money.
do: Claim early.
Get any holding period confirmed in writing.

entries.title: Unclaimed-money check, step by step
entries.take: A short pass to find money held for you. It follows what each collector's own page and the Copyright Office survey describe.

entries.title: Minimum notice before a US unclaimed distribution
entries.unit: days of public notice before a distribution
entries.take: Section 115 sets this as the least advance warning the MLC must give the industry before it pays out unclaimed money.

entries.title: Music collections reported to CISAC societies for 2022
entries.take: Scale only: gross music collections before deductions. The report gives no unclaimed total, so do not read this as money waiting.

entries.title: Tracks on PPL's repertoire database
entries.take: PPL says its database holds more than this many tracks, so searching it for your recordings is worthwhile.

usc-115.publisher: United States Congress (Cornell LII copy of the U.S. Code)
usc-115.title: 17 U.S.C. 115: Scope of exclusive rights in nondramatic musical works, compulsory license for making and distributing phonorecords
usc-115.support: Subsections (a) and (b) on eligibility and notices; (d) on the blanket license, MLC duties, holding, distribution of unclaimed accrued royalties, songwriter share and audits.
usc-115.edition: Title 17, section 115, as shown by LII

usco-unclaimed-study.title: Unclaimed Royalties: Best Practice Recommendations for the Mechanical Licensing Collective
usco-unclaimed-study.support: Front matter reproduces MMA sec. 102(f) (substantial weight). Executive summary: hold beyond the statutory minimum, no first distribution for at least five years, independent verification of market-share calculations.
usco-unclaimed-study.edition: Report of the Register of Copyrights, July 2021

mlc-tools.title: The MLC's Tools
mlc-tools.support: Public Work Search (more than 55 million songs), Claiming, Works Registration, Matching, Overclaims, Catalog Export and Transfer tools; check the Claiming Tool before registering; keep banking and tax details current.

mlc-unclaimed.title: Unclaimed Accrued Royalties
mlc-unclaimed.support: Defines unclaimed accrued royalties as unmatched plus unclaimed; intends to begin distributions in April 2027 through market share, starting with January 2021 blanket usage; dashboard for 2021 usage.

mlc-missing-members.title: Missing Member Lookup
mlc-missing-members.support: Searchable list of rightsholders not yet Members who may be owed US digital audio mechanicals; excludes historical unmatched royalties; Get Started block says connecting with the MLC is free.

sx-owed.title: Artists, Labels & Producers
sx-owed.support: 'Are you owed royalties?' section: registration needed to be paid; search tool; four status lists; registering free; SX Direct free, used to search and claim recordings; no time limit. Read with WebFetch.

cmrra-unclaimed.title: Unclaimed Works Portal for Online Music Services
cmrra-unclaimed.support: CMRRA Direct account needed (approval up to 3 business days); match recordings and add missing shares via the Unclaimed Works menu; quarterly invoicing for past and current use; no fee or deadline. Read with WebFetch.

ppl-performers.title: Performers
ppl-performers.support: Performer claim via myPPL if not on line-up; may need evidence; missing track: ask rightsholder; repertoire and played or broadcast; qualification by residence, citizenship or place; UK 70-year ER right. Read with WebFetch.

butler-cmo-2020.publisher: U.S. Copyright Office (report commissioned from Susan P. Butler)
butler-cmo-2020.title: Collective Rights Management Practices Around the World: A Survey of CMO Practices to Reduce the Occurrence of Unclaimed Royalties in Musical Works
butler-cmo-2020.support: Sec. 4 sources of data; sec. 5B reasons CMOs cannot match; sec. 6 lists, thresholds, manual research; match-rate remarks; sec. 7 suspense accounts and pre-matching; sec. 9 ways unclaimed money is distributed; social and cultural deductions.
butler-cmo-2020.edition: Butler, April 2020; CMOs anonymous, information gathered January to April 2020

wipo-cmo-music.title: Educational Material on Collective Management of Copyright and Related Rights, Module 2: Management of copyright and related rights in the field of music
wipo-cmo-music.support: Sec. 3.4: a CMO needs full documentation of works and rights holders to distribute; sec. 3.6: social and cultural deductions to be agreed in advance; sec. 3.7: ISWC, IPI.

cisac-gcr-2023.title: Global Collections Report 2023 (for 2022 data)
cisac-gcr-2023.support: Music collections 10.83 bn EUR in 2022, up 28.0%; methodology: gross collections before deductions for administration, cultural or social purposes; 225 societies in 116 countries or territories.
